question: Why is Earth's gravity, 9.81 m/s², so close to π squared, 9.87? Lengthen a pendulum and time one swing.
answer: Because the metre nearly was a pendulum. One swing takes π times the square root of length over g, so a one-second swing needs a length of g/π² metres. In 1791 the French Academy weighed that as the new unit, then chose a ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator arc instead; the two landed within 0.6%.
move: When two numbers match too well, look for a shared history before calling it luck.
ask: When two things match too neatly, do I look for a shared cause before calling it luck?
source: Alder, The Measure of All Things, 2002
reference: Alder, The Measure of All Things: The Seven-Year Odyssey and Hidden Error That Transformed the World, Free Press, 2002

notes.text: A quarter of a metre: half a second per swing.
99.4 cm: one swing, one second. That length is g ÷ π² metres.
Two metres: 1.42 s. Four times the half metre, only twice the swing.
